title: Derived Data with Selectors
description: Learn how to compute and cache derived data from Redux state using selectors and memoization.

data.text: In Redux, you store your application's state, not every possible view of that state. **Derived data** is information you can calculate from the raw state. Instead of storing computed values, you compute them when needed using selectors.

For example, if you store an array of orders, the total price is derived data. If you store a list of users, the count of active users is derived. The key principle is: **don't duplicate data that can be computed**.

Storing computed values in state leads to synchronization problems. When the source data changes, you must remember to update all the places that duplicate it. This creates bugs where the UI shows stale data.

cards.title: Duplicated in State
cards.content:
Must sync manually on every update
Risk of stale data inconsistencies
Harder to reason about source of truth
More state to maintain
Potential bugs from missed updates

cards.title: Derived with Selectors
cards.content:
Always up-to-date automatically
Single source of truth preserved
Impossible to get out of sync
Computed on-demand efficiently
Memoization prevents recalculation

data.text: A selector is a function that extracts data from the Redux state. Simple selectors just return a slice of state. More complex selectors compute derived values.

data.title: Simple vs Derived Selectors

data.text: The problem with simple selectors is that they recompute on every render, even when the inputs haven't changed. For expensive computations, this wastes CPU cycles. For object or array returns, it creates new references every time, causing unnecessary re-renders.

data.caption: Selector memoization behavior
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Component Renders] --> B{same inputs?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Return cached result]
    B -->|No| D[Compute new result]
    D --> E[Cache new result]
    E --> F[Return computed value]
    C --> G[No re-render needed]

data.text: **`createSelector`** from Reselect (included with Redux Toolkit) creates memoized selectors. It only recomputes when one of its input selectors returns a new value. For primitive comparisons, it uses `===`. For objects and arrays, it does a shallow comparison.

data.title: Memoized Selectors

data.text: Selectors compose naturally. You can build complex derived data by combining simpler selectors. This makes your code reusable and testable.

data.title: Composing Selectors
data.content: Building complex selectors from simple ones

data.text: Some computations are expensive: sorting large lists, filtering thousands of items, or processing complex data structures. Memoization helps, but you should also consider when and where these computations happen.

data.title: Expensive Operations
Shallow Comparison Gotcha
data.text: createSelector uses shallow equality for comparisons. If you return a new object every time (even with the same contents), it won't memoize. Always return the same object reference when the contents haven't changed.

terms.definition: A function that extracts and computes data from Redux state.
Values that can be calculated from other state, not stored separately.
Caching a computation's result and returning it when inputs haven't changed.
A function that creates memoized selectors from input selectors and an output function.
Checking if two values are the same reference using ===.

data.title: Build a Dashboard Selector
data.description: Create memoized selectors for an analytics dashboard that computes various metrics from raw event data.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Store raw state, not computed values
Use selectors to derive data from state
Selectors compose naturally into complex derivations
data.takeaway: Selectors with memoization keep your state minimal while providing efficient access to computed values.
